questions.prompt: A manager says, "The dashboard covers everything important, so we don't need to look at individual cases." What confusion is the chapter warning about?
choices: Mistaking a representation for the full reality
Collecting too much data before acting
Giving customers too much influence over operations

explanation.gentle: Yes. The dashboard may still be useful, but it is still a map. The danger is acting as if the reduced picture contains the whole terrain.
explanation.direct: That statement collapses map into territory. The chapter argues that summaries help only while their omissions remain visible.
explanation.competitive: The trap is giving a proxy the status of reality itself. That is how clean signals start making expensive calls.

questions.prompt: Why does the Bezos customer-service story matter so much in this chapter?
choices: It proves anecdotes should always replace data
It shows a direct territory check exposing a misleading metric
It argues that customer service is the most important department

explanation.gentle: Right. The point is not to reject metrics. It is to compare the metric with what the metric claims to represent.
explanation.direct: The story matters because a live check against the ground revealed that the dashboard's picture was incomplete.
explanation.competitive: The metric lost authority the moment real contact broke it. That is the chapter's mechanism in miniature.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest reason Newton and Einstein appear in the chapter together?
choices: To show that newer models always erase older ones completely
To show that science is mostly a contest of personalities
To show that a model can stay useful within a range even after its limits become clear

explanation.gentle: Exactly. The chapter is teaching bounded trust, not all-or-nothing trust.
explanation.direct: Newton remained useful while Einstein defined conditions the older map could not cover well enough.
explanation.competitive: The win is range control. A strong model is still not a universal passport.

questions.prompt: Jordan runs a warehouse where the "orders processed" metric keeps improving, but damaged shipments are rising. What move best matches the chapter?
choices: Keep the metric and add a direct check on what customers receive
Ignore all metrics for the next month and rely on intuition
Assume the damage reports are emotional noise compared with hard numbers

explanation.gentle: Good call. The chapter does not ask Jordan to throw away maps. It asks for a better test against the territory.
explanation.direct: Orders processed is a proxy. The right move is to compare it with the actual outcome that matters rather than trusting the proxy alone.
explanation.competitive: Keep the scorecard, but strip it of undeserved authority until it survives contact with the ground.

questions.prompt: A dean says a ranking system is fair because it uses the same formula for every department. What important question is still missing?
choices: Whether the formula was expensive to build
Who designed the ranking and what it was built to reward
Whether faculty members like the published results

explanation.gentle: Yes. Equal treatment inside a formula does not make the formula neutral.
explanation.direct: The cartographer question matters because the builder decided what counted and what stayed invisible.
explanation.competitive: A neutral-looking instrument still carries priorities. The builder's incentives are part of the map.

questions.prompt: Why is "maps can influence territories" a stronger warning than "maps can be wrong"?
choices: Because it shows the model can start shaping behavior and outcomes
Because it means people should avoid planning entirely
Because it says descriptions are more dangerous than commands

explanation.gentle: Right. Once rewards or attention attach to a representation, people begin adapting to it.
explanation.direct: The chapter moves from descriptive error to causal distortion: the proxy can start steering the world around itself.
explanation.competitive: Wrong maps mislead. Powerful maps train the game to flatter the map.

questions.prompt: Leah reads a cold text from a friend and instantly decides the friendship is in trouble. Which response best applies the model?
choices: Trust the feeling because first reactions are usually honest
Check directly before treating the small signal as the whole relationship
Ignore the text completely because all interpretation is unreliable

explanation.gentle: Exactly. A short message can matter, but it is still a thin map of a much larger territory.
explanation.direct: The model points toward direct contact when a narrow cue is getting more authority than it deserves.
explanation.competitive: Break the proxy's monopoly before four words take over the entire story.

questions.prompt: A product team notices that its planning board rewards easy ticket closure, so hard infrastructure work keeps slipping. What does this reveal?
choices: The board is tracking real progress more accurately than the engineers admit
The team needs more optimism during sprint planning
The representation is changing behavior in ways that distort the underlying work

explanation.gentle: Yes. The board is no longer just describing progress. It is reshaping what people choose to do.
explanation.direct: This is the chapter's third rule in action: the map has become a behavioral force.
explanation.competitive: The scorecard has started rewriting the game, which means the proxy now needs redesign.

questions.prompt: Which position best captures the chapter's hard boundary condition around maps?
choices: All abstractions should be treated with suspicion because direct experience is always superior
Useful abstractions are necessary, but their authority should stay provisional and range-limited
A good model eventually becomes more reliable than the reality it summarizes

explanation.gentle: That is the balanced reading. You need maps, but you also need a way to keep them answerable to the world.
explanation.direct: The chapter rejects both map worship and map rejection. It argues for bounded trust under feedback.
explanation.competitive: The mature move is disciplined use, not romantic anti-model posturing and not blind faith.

questions.prompt: If this chapter makes you more cautious about borrowed maps, what question naturally sets up the next chapter?
choices: How can I tell where my own judgment is dependable and where it is not?
How can I stop using all models and rely only on firsthand experience?
How can I build a single perfect model that avoids revision?

explanation.gentle: Nicely done. Once borrowed pictures look partial, the next useful question is where your own understanding is solid enough to trust.
explanation.direct: The bridge is competence. After map-versus-territory, the next issue is the range of your own reliable judgment.
explanation.competitive: This model strips away borrowed certainty. The next chapter asks where your own range actually ends.
